To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the passage encoder has a stronger influence on generalization than the question encoder in DPR; (ii) the question encoder is more important for the upper bound while the passage encoder is more important to the lower bound; (iii) the question encoder has a larger impact on generalization when the question distribution is closer to the passage distribution, while the passage encoder has larger impact when the question distribution has a larger variance; (iv) the passage encoder is less affected by the question distribution,
the passage encoder of DPR has more influence on generalization than the question encoder and that the passage encoder is more sensitive to OOD data.

1) The passage encoder has more impact on the lower bound and question encoder has more impact the upper bound of generalization; 2) Applying an OOD passage/passage encoder usually hurts the lower bound of retrieval accuracy while an out of distribution question/question encoder sometimes even improves it; 3) The performance gap between IND and OOD question encoders is smaller than the performance gap between IND passage encoders and OOD passage encoders.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the question and passage encoders of DPR are not interchangeable and their adaptation is not a one size fits all solution.
we should not blindly use an IND encoder for OOD QA, but instead carefully consider the encoder's effect on generalization.
